StudyVault · diagram pipeline · 8 September 2026

Line and wash,
and one house style

One style for every diagram on the site. Variety comes from composition, not from style. The ink carries the information; the wash carries only material colour and mood — so the drawing has to survive having its colour taken away.

1Style block
8Composition forms
6 / 8Gate accepted
7 / 8Ink test passed
21pTotal, 18 images

The locked style block fixed text, appended verbatim to every brief

Written once. It never varies by image, by subject or by lesson. {accent} is units.accent from Supabase, and it is the only thing in the block that changes.

Style - the StudyVault house style. It is the same for every diagram on the site; only the composition changes.

Draw it as a hand-drawn line-and-wash illustration on warm off-white paper (#faf8f5), in the manner of a painted natural-history plate: confident dark ink outlines of one consistent pen weight throughout, laid over loose translucent watercolour washes with visible brush edges and a little paper grain. Wash the shadows; never block them in as flat tone.

THE INK CARRIES THE INFORMATION. Every structure, boundary, division, label, leader line, arrow, tick, number and hatch is drawn in ink. The wash carries only material colour and mood. Nothing may be told by colour alone: if two things must be told apart, the ink must tell them apart - by an outline, a hatch, a stipple or a written label - and the wash may then agree with the ink. The finished drawing must stay completely legible with every colour removed.

Labels: a clear humanist sans-serif, one size for every label, set horizontally in the accent colour {accent}, each joined to the thing it names by a thin ink leader line ending in a small dot on the structure itself. The accent colour {accent} is for chrome only - label text, leader lines, arrows, tick marks, axis marks and numbered discs. It never colours the drawn matter.

Colour: physical materials, objects, places, buildings and clothing keep their natural, period-appropriate colours, slightly desaturated as watercolour on rag paper (rock browns and greys, magma orange-red, water blue, vegetation green, oxygenated blood red, deoxygenated blood blue). Abstract shapes with no natural colour take soft neutral grey washes.

Composition: generous margins on all four sides, one clear subject, plenty of unpainted paper, no clutter, no photographic realism, no drop shadows, no logos, no watermarks.

Never: a title, a caption, a key or a legend inside the picture; any free-floating sentence that is not attached to a leader line; a faceless, blank or featureless person (people appear only as ordinary anonymous figures with normal faces); a real identifiable named person; an exam-board name. Spelling is British English, and any lettering drawn on an object must be a real, correctly spelled word appropriate to the date and place shown.

The composition catalogue the brief agent picks exactly one, and none always counts

This is where the variety lives. The chosen form’s composition text goes into the prompt above the label and fact lists; the style block goes below them. The forms are not a sequence and carry no order.

ribbon-timeline

Use when the order of events over time, and the gaps between them, carry the meaning.

A ribbon or a road runs left to right across the frame, inked on both edges and washed softly along its length. Each event sits on the ribbon at its own inked tick and dot: a small vignette above the tick, the date and the event name labelled below it. Nothing floats free of the ribbon; every leader reaches its own dot.

document-stack

Use when a sequence of stages each produces a document, a record or a front page.

Four to six sheets - front pages, forms, letters or cards - drawn overlapping in a staggered fan from top-left to bottom-right, each far enough clear of the next to show its own inked heading. A numbered accent disc on each sheet gives the reading order. The papers keep their natural paper colour; only the discs and labels take the accent.

cutaway

Use when the inside of a thing explains it and the outside hides it.

The object is drawn whole and in proportion, with a wedge or the near face cut away so the interior is seen in section. Cut surfaces are hatched in ink at a single angle; interior parts are washed in their natural colours and outlined; every named part sends a leader out to a label in the margin.

exploded-view

Use when the parts fit together and their arrangement or order is the point.

The parts are drawn separated along one common axis in assembly order, each floating clear of the next with paper between them, and a thin dashed ink line running through all of them showing where each part returns. Each part is inked and washed as its own material.

then-and-now

Use when a change is the point and both the before and the after can be drawn.

One frame divided by a single vertical ink rule into two panels of equal width, drawn from an identical viewpoint at an identical scale so that only what has changed differs between them. Each panel carries its date as a label; the changed features are labelled in the panel where they appear.

map-with-vignettes

Use when place carries the meaning - where things are, or what happens where.

An outline map with inked coastlines and borders and flat pale washes for land and sea, and three to six small vignettes set in the sea or the margin around it, each tied to its position on the map by a thin ink leader ending in a dot. Place names are labelled on the map itself.

annotated-object

Use when one thing has named parts and the parts are the lesson.

A single object, room or interior drawn large and centred, filling most of the frame, in straight-on or three-quarter view, inked in full and washed in its natural materials. Every named part carries a leader out to a label in the surrounding margin; the labels sit clear of the drawing, not on top of it.

data-picture

Use when one number series, or the shape of one curve, carries the point.

A real chart drawn by hand: inked axes with inked tick marks and an honest scale, the quantity and its unit named along each axis, bars or curves inked in outline and filled with one flat translucent wash, and every value printed at its own bar or point. No decoration, no vignette, no illustration beside the chart.

none

Use when the lesson is an argument, an ethical debate or a piece of literary analysis with nothing physical to draw.

No picture. A forced picture is worse than no picture; the lesson is fine without a figure.

One image per form a different real lesson each, one attempt unless the gate asked for a correction

Eight live lessons across eight subject families, briefed the way the pipeline’s brief agent writes them, composed with the catalogue form and the locked block. Every picture is judged twice: by the vision gate in the context of the lesson text, and then again with all of its colour stripped out.

ribbon-timeline

History · Germany in Transition, 1919-1939

The Stresemann years: a 'golden age'?

history-eduqas · lesson 3 · accent #374151 · ribbon timeline of the Stresemann years, 1924-1929

The brief

A ribbon running left to right from 1924 to 1929 carrying the milestones of the Stresemann era in order: the Dawes Plan of 1924 (a vignette of American dollars flowing into a German factory), the Locarno Pact of 1925 (a vignette of a signed treaty with its wax seal), Germany joining the League of Nations in 1926 (a vignette of a flag being raised beside an assembly building), the Young Plan of 1929 (a vignette of a reduced stack of reparation coins), and, crowded together at the far right end, Stresemann's death in October 1929 and the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 (a vignette of a falling share-price line).

Why a picture here
The 'golden age' argument turns on how closely Stresemann's death sits to the Wall Street Crash after five years of recovery, which only a timeline of the milestones makes visible.
Labels that must appear
Dawes Plan, 1924; Locarno Pact, 1925; League of Nations, 1926; Young Plan, 1929; Stresemann's death, October 1929; Wall Street Crash, October 1929
Facts the gate will check
  • the ribbon runs left to right from 1924 to 1929 with a tick and a dot beneath every event
  • the Dawes Plan tick comes before the Young Plan tick
  • Stresemann's death and the Wall Street Crash sit on adjacent ticks at the far right end of the ribbon

Vision gate & ink test

Both faults from attempt one are gone. The 1926 vignette now raises a plain navy banner on a ball-finial pole beside a neoclassical assembly building, with no United Nations wreath-and-globe and no other post-1926 device; the crowd below is drawn from behind in period homburgs, bowlers and a cloche. The fifth vignette is now an empty upholstered armchair with a black crepe swag over its back and white lilies at its foot, so no named person appears anywhere in the frame. The ribbon runs left to right, inked on both edges with a soft parchment wash and scrolled ends, and each of the six events carries a dot on the top edge, a tick crossing the ribbon, a dot on the lower edge and a leader to a terminal dot above its own label; all six labels read exactly as required and are correctly spelled, including "Stresemann's death, October 1929" and "Wall Street Crash, October 1929" on the last two adjacent ticks. Dawes 1924 sits first and Young 1929 fourth, and the Young Plan vignette now teaches the reduction properly with a tall coin stack, an inked arrow and a short stack; period detail holds throughout (dollar notes into a red-brick German works with a rail wagon, a dip pen and a red wax seal on the "LOCARNO PACT / TREATY" sheet, 1929 fedoras before a "New York Stock Exchange" board).

First attempt was a retry — gateThe flag raised in the League of Nations vignette is the United Nations flag (blue field, white polar world map, olive-branch wreath) - an emblem created in 1946, twenty years after the event labelled beneath it

The one correction sent backDelete the United Nations emblem from the raised flag in the 1926 vignette and redraw that flag as a plain undevised ceremonial banner, and replace the fifth vignette's portrait head with an unpeopled mourning still life (an empty Foreign Office chair draped with the black crepe sash, the lilies kept as drawn), leaving every other vignette, tick, dot, leader and label exactly where it is.
  • The League building's architrave carries four faint word-shaped smudges that imitate a carved inscription; no glyph resolves and nothing is readable at delivery size, but it is simulated lettering on a drawn object.
  • The banner is undevised, so the vignette depends entirely on its label to say which body Germany joined in 1926; the picture alone shows only a flag-raising.
  • The lower third of the frame is empty paper, so the whole drawing sits high in the crop.
  • House rule: Lettering rule, marginal: imitation inscription on the League building frieze (sub-legible, no misreadable word). Every other piece of lettering in the frame is a real, correctly spelled, period-appropriate word.

Ink test. With the colour gone every tick, dot, leader and label still reads, the ribbon still separates from the ground by its inked edges and wash, the crepe-draped chair and white lilies still say mourning, and the falling share line stays the heaviest stroke on its grid.

document-stack

Business · Human Resources

Recruitment & Selection

business-aqa · lesson 2 · accent #7c3aed · staggered stack of recruitment documents in sequence

The brief

Five sheets of paper fanned in order, each headed and each showing a few ruled lines of writing: a job analysis worksheet, a job description sheet listing duties, a person specification sheet listing skills and qualities, a printed job advertisement, and a curriculum vitae. The papers are ordinary office white and cream, drawn as if laid on a desk.

Why a picture here
The selection process is a chain in which each stage produces a specific document, and students routinely muddle the job description with the person specification; a stack of the actual papers in order fixes both the order and the difference.
Labels that must appear
job analysis; job description; person specification; job advert; CV screening
Facts the gate will check
  • the five sheets are numbered 1 to 5 in reading order, starting with job analysis and ending with CV screening
  • the job description sheet lists duties and the person specification sheet lists skills and qualities, so the two are visibly different documents
  • the job advert sheet comes after both the job description and the person specification

Vision gate & ink test

Five sheets fan from top-left to bottom-right, each clear enough of the next to show its whole heading: Job Analysis Worksheet (Purpose of the job, Key outputs, Working conditions), Job Description (Job title, Department, Reports to, then a bulleted Duties list), Person Specification (bulleted Skills, then bulleted Qualities), Job Advert (a boxed advert reading 'We're looking for a reliable and motivated team member', 'Join our friendly team and help us make a difference. Full training provided.', bullets Competitive salary / Flexible hours / Great career development, and a grey 'Apply now' button) and Curriculum Vitae (Personal details with Name, Address, Telephone, Email; Education; Work experience; 'References available on request'). Five purple discs numbered 1 to 5 sit clear of the papers, each with a short leader ending in a purple dot exactly on its own sheet's top-left corner - disc 2's dot lands on the Job Description sheet, not on the Job Analysis sheet overlapping it, and disc 3's lands on the Person Specification, so no leader strays onto a neighbour. The accent purple is confined to the discs, their numerals, the leaders, the terminal dots and the five labels; the papers stay office white and cream and the Apply now button is grey, so no drawn matter takes the accent. The sequence matches the lesson exactly - job analysis feeds a job description of duties and a person specification of skills and qualities, then the advert, then CV screening - and the duties/skills split is visibly different between sheets 2 and 3, which is the distinction students most often collapse. All lettering is real and British: Curriculum Vitae, Job Advert, Person Specification, Personal details, Work experience, References available on request.

  • A stray dark ink speck sits in the top-left background at roughly (74, 14), attached to nothing
  • On the CV the ruled lines run one longer than their labels: four field labels (Name, Address, Telephone, Email) carry five rules, and each of the Education and Work experience blocks shows three bullets against four rules
  • The rules on the CV sit low against their labels, so each line reads as belonging to the field below rather than beside it
  • House rule: Composition rule, minor: the rule says a numbered accent disc sits on each sheet, but all five discs float clear of the papers in the background and reach their sheet by a short leader instead

Ink test. Colour removed, every sheet is still told from its neighbour by its inked outline and cast shadow, all five discs still read as filled discs with legible reversed numerals, every leader and terminal dot stays followable to its own corner, and all headings and body lettering stay crisp - the only thing lost is the cream-versus-white paper tint, which carried no meaning.

cutaway

Biology · Biology Paper 1

The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

science-aqa · lesson 4 · accent #16a34a · cutaway of the human heart

The brief

The human heart drawn whole in three-quarter view with the near wall cut away so all four chambers are seen in section: right atrium and right ventricle on the left of the picture as the reader looks at it, left atrium and left ventricle on the right, with the vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and aorta entering and leaving. Ink arrows trace the direction of blood through the chambers and out of the vessels. The muscle wall of the left ventricle is drawn visibly thicker than that of the right ventricle.

Why a picture here
A cutaway heart with flow arrows makes the double circulatory system and the chamber order immediately clear, which is the hardest part of this lesson to hold in the head from text alone.
Labels that must appear
right atrium; right ventricle; left atrium; left ventricle; vena cava; pulmonary artery; pulmonary vein; aorta
Facts the gate will check
  • arrows run vena cava into right atrium, into right ventricle, out through the pulmonary artery
  • arrows run pulmonary vein into left atrium, into left ventricle, out through the aorta
  • the left ventricle wall is drawn thicker than the right ventricle wall
  • deoxygenated blood is washed blue and oxygenated blood red, but every vessel is also named in ink so the picture reads without the colour

Vision gate & ink test

All eight required labels are present and the left ventricle wall is drawn visibly thicker than the right, and the right-heart chain still reads correctly: vena cava down into the right atrium, through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and out along the blue arch to the pulmonary artery mouth. The left heart is still wrong, and in new ways. At the left atrium a single fat arrow forks into two heads, one driving up and out into the upper pulmonary vein and one driving back down into the atrium, so the retry note's reversal was not made; a second double-headed arrow sits wholly inside the atrium pointing both left and right. The big left ventricle arrow rises through the mitral valve leaflets and its head lands inside the left atrium - ventricle-to-atrium backflow - while the ascending aorta arrow floats unattached in the aortic root, so the ventricle still never connects to the aorta. The 'left atrium' leader dot lands on the cut rim of the middle pulmonary vein stub rather than on the chamber (attempt one had this leader right), the unlabelled blue vessel low on the outer wall was not deleted, and the stipple has been laid over the aorta and all three pulmonary veins as heavily as over the vena cava and right heart.

First attempt was a retry — gate and ink testuppermost pulmonary vein flow arrow is reversed: it points from the left atrium out into the vessel, contradicting the lesson's flow sequence

The one correction sent backRedraw only the left-heart flow arrows: reverse the arrow at the upper pulmonary vein so it runs from the vessel into the left atrium, and carry the left ventricle arrow up through the aortic valve to join the existing arrow in the ascending aorta. Delete the second, unlabelled vena cava that enters low on the outer wall. AND ADD THE INK THIS PICTURE IS MISSING, because it failed the ink test: fill every deoxygenated space (vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery) with an even ink stipple, and leave every oxygenated space (pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta) clear of stipple, so the two sides are told apart by ink and stay told apart when the red and blue wash is removed. Hatch every cut surface at one single angle. Keep every other line, label, valve and wash exactly as it is.
  • Upper pulmonary vein arrow still runs out of the left atrium into the vessel, and is now double-headed, so it asserts both directions at once
  • Second double-headed arrow inside the left atrium body gives no direction of flow
  • Left ventricle arrow runs up through the mitral valve and ends inside the left atrium - ventricle-to-atrium backflow
  • Ascending aorta arrow starts floating in the aortic root, unconnected to the left ventricle, so required fact 2 (pulmonary vein into left atrium, into left ventricle, out through the aorta) is not shown
  • 'left atrium' leader dot lands on the cut rim of the middle pulmonary vein stub, not on the atrial chamber - a regression from attempt one
  • Unlabelled second blue vessel low on the outer wall was not deleted
  • Stipple applied to the aorta and all three pulmonary veins as well as the deoxygenated side, so the ink no longer separates the two circuits
  • A vertical arrow in the right ventricle starts at the pulmonary outflow and points down into the cavity, contradicting the outflow arrow beside it
  • Stray green leader dots left floating inside the middle and lower pulmonary vein stubs; the pulmonary artery leader terminates in two dots
  • The 'f' of 'left atrium' is drawn half-erased; at the delivered 900px JPEG it reads 'lert atrium', and the full-resolution 1536px PNG confirms a broken, pale glyph rather than clean lettering
  • House rule: cutaway composition rule: cut surfaces are not hatched at a single angle - the hatch follows each wall's contour, running near-vertical on the left ventricle free wall, steeply diagonal across the septum and near-radial around the lower outer wall
  • House rule: cutaway composition rule: 'left atrium' does not lead out to the part it names, its leader landing on a pulmonary vein stub instead
  • House rule: real, correctly spelled lettering: 'left' is drawn with a broken 'f' and reads as 'lert' at delivery resolution

Ink test. With the colour gone the stipple covers the aorta and all three pulmonary veins exactly as it covers the vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary artery, so it marks nothing in particular and a reader cannot tell deoxygenated blood from oxygenated blood by ink alone.

exploded-view

Computer Science · Computer Systems

Memory and Storage

computer-science-aqa · lesson 3 · accent #b91c1c · exploded view of a computer's memory and storage

The brief

The storage of a desktop computer drawn exploded along one axis running from the processor outwards, in the order the data travels: the CPU package with its registers and cache drawn on the chip itself, then a RAM module, then a small ROM chip, then a solid-state drive, then a hard disk drive with its platter and read-write arm visible. Each part floats clear of the next on a dashed assembly line, drawn in its own material: green board, silver-grey metal, dark chip plastic. An inked bracket gathers the RAM and ROM together and a second inked bracket gathers the two drives together.

Why a picture here
Students learn RAM, ROM, cache and secondary storage as a list of definitions; drawing them separated along the path the data actually travels shows why the CPU cannot reach the hard drive directly.
Labels that must appear
registers; cache; RAM; ROM; solid-state drive; hard disk drive; primary storage; secondary storage
Facts the gate will check
  • registers and cache are drawn on the CPU itself, not as separate boards
  • RAM and ROM sit inside the bracket labelled primary storage and the solid-state drive and hard disk drive sit inside the bracket labelled secondary storage
  • the hard disk drive shows a circular platter and a read-write arm
  • the parts are ordered from the CPU outwards, so primary storage sits between the CPU and secondary storage

Vision gate & ink test

The five parts sit on one axis in the order the lesson gives, CPU package, RAM DIMM, ROM chip, solid-state drive, then hard disk, each floating clear of the next with paper between them and a thin dashed accent line running through all of them and out to an arrowhead on the right. Registers and cache are drawn as two blocks on the processor's own silver die, each with its own leader landing inside its block, so the 'on the CPU itself' fact reads correctly rather than as separate boards. The primary storage bracket spans exactly the RAM module and the ROM chip, and the secondary storage bracket spans exactly the SSD and the hard disk, its arms aligned with their outer edges. The hard disk is opened to show a circular platter with its spindle hub, plus an actuator arm on its pivot bearing with the voice-coil magnet behind it. Each part is inked and washed as its own material (green board, silver-grey metal, black chip plastic), the accent red carries only labels, leaders, brackets and the dashed axis, and all eight required labels are present, correctly spelled and correctly landed.

  • the primary storage bracket gathers only RAM and ROM, while the lesson's key fact counts registers and cache as primary storage too - an omission rather than a false claim, and the grouping the brief required
  • the CPU package itself carries no label, so the green square is identified only by the registers and cache blocks drawn on it
  • illegible faux small print sits under 'SSD' on the drive label, and faint faux silkscreen runs along the RAM board
  • House rule: lettering rule: faux small print that is not a real word is drawn under 'SSD' on the drive label and as silkscreen along the RAM board; both are sub-pixel smudges at the delivered 900px width and do not resolve into letterforms

Ink test. Every part stays separable by silhouette and outline, the dashed axis and both brackets stay visible, and every leader still lands on its target, so no distinction the lesson needs was ever carried by the colour.

then-and-now

Geography · Paper 1: Physical Geography

Coastal Management: The Holderness Coast

geography-aqa · lesson 16 · accent #4f46e5 · then-and-now split of the coast at Mappleton and Cowden

The brief

One frame split by a vertical rule into two panels of the same stretch of the Holderness coast, drawn from the same viewpoint and at the same scale, looking along the coast with Mappleton on the left of each panel and Cowden three kilometres south on the right. Left panel, 1990: a continuous boulder-clay cliff with a narrow beach running unbroken past both places, and an arrow along the shore showing longshore drift carrying sediment south. Right panel, today: two rock groynes and a concrete sea wall at Mappleton with a wide beach piled up on their northern side, and at Cowden a cut-back cliff with a slumped face, a bare narrow beach and a bungalow standing close to the cliff edge.

Why a picture here
The Mappleton scheme is the lesson's whole argument that protecting one place damages another, and the argument only becomes obvious when the same stretch of coast is drawn before and after the defences.
Labels that must appear
Mappleton; Cowden; 1990; today; longshore drift; sea wall; rock groynes; wide beach; beach starved of sediment; cliff retreat
Facts the gate will check
  • both panels are drawn from the same viewpoint at the same scale, so only the defences and the beach differ
  • in the right-hand panel the beach at Mappleton is wide and the beach at Cowden is narrow
  • the longshore drift arrow runs from Mappleton towards Cowden in both panels
  • the cliff at Cowden has retreated further inland in the right-hand panel than in the left

Vision gate & ink test

The retry was carried out. The 'sea wall' leader now ends in a dot sitting squarely on the grey concrete wall face, a little above the sand and well clear of the cottages behind it, and the wall itself is drawn as a banded concrete structure with a clear capping line. The two attempt-one faults that went with it are also gone: the 'today' panel no longer carries a twenty-house terrace that the 1990 panel lacked (both panels now show the same small cluster of Mappleton cottages), and the 'wide beach' leader carries a single dot instead of a doubled one. The panels sit either side of a single vertical ink rule at x=768 of 1536, are of equal width, and the sea horizon matches to within about 3 px, so the viewpoint holds; the beach at Mappleton in the right panel is plainly two to three times the width of the bare, bouldery strip at Cowden, the Cowden cliff is cut back so far that the bungalow stands on the very lip where in 1990 it had a field's width of ground in front of it, and the longshore drift arrow runs from Mappleton down-coast towards Cowden in both panels. All ten labels are present and correctly spelled in British English, 'rock groynes' included, and every leader dot lands on the matter it names; I read the lettering on the 1536 px PNG as well as the 900 px JPEG. What is still wrong is the groyne mechanism: measured on the PNG, the water reaches the foot of each groyne on its northern, up-drift side and the sand piles up on its southern, down-drift side, which is the reverse of what a drift running north to south would build.

First attempt was a retry — gate'sea wall' leader dot lands on the terraced houses, not on the concrete wall it names

The one correction sent backMove the dot at the end of the 'sea wall' leader down off the terraced housing and onto the grey concrete wall itself, so it sits on the wall face just above the sand, and leave every other line, label, arrow and wash exactly as drawn.
  • sediment is drawn accreting on the southern, down-drift face of both rock groynes while the longshore drift arrow runs north to south, so the trapped beach is on the wrong side of the structures (carried over unfixed from attempt one, which the retry note did not ask to correct)
  • the Cowden bungalow is drawn about 14 per cent wider and about 38 px lower in the 'today' panel than in the 1990 panel, so the two panels are not at exactly the same scale even though the horizon matches
  • 'longshore drift' carries no leader or dot in either panel; it sits beside the arrow it names and relies on proximity alone
  • House rule: composition rule 'drawn from an identical viewpoint at an identical scale' - the Cowden bungalow, an unchanged feature, is about 14 per cent larger and sits about 38 px lower in the right-hand panel

Ink test. With the colour gone the sea keeps its horizontal wave strokes, the beach stays a pale smooth band edged by a white surf line, the cliff face keeps its vertical fluting, the sea wall reads as a banded mid-grey structure with a hard capping line and the rock groynes as dark stippled masses, so every labelled part, every leader dot and both arrows still read from ink alone.

map-with-vignettes

Physics · Physics Paper 1

Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

separate-sciences · lesson 2 · accent #dc2626 · map of the United Kingdom's energy resources

The brief

An outline map of the United Kingdom with small vignettes set in the surrounding sea, each tied by a leader to the place it belongs: an offshore wind farm off the east coast of England, a hydroelectric dam in the Scottish Highlands, a tidal barrage across the Severn Estuary in the south-west, a field of solar panels in south-east England, a gas-fired power station on the Humber, and a nuclear power station on the Somerset coast. The land is washed a flat pale green and the sea a flat pale blue.

Why a picture here
The lesson says renewable resources are location-dependent and weather-dependent but never shows where they are; a map is the one thing that makes 'location-dependent' concrete.
Labels that must appear
offshore wind; hydroelectric; tidal; solar; natural gas; nuclear; renewable; non-renewable
Facts the gate will check
  • the hydroelectric vignette is tied to the mountains of northern Scotland and the tidal vignette to the estuary in the south-west
  • the wind, hydroelectric, tidal and solar vignettes are marked renewable and the natural gas and nuclear vignettes are marked non-renewable, in ink and not by colour alone
  • the solar vignette is tied to the south-east of England, further south than the wind vignette

Vision gate & ink test

Both parts of the retry were carried out. The Bristol Channel now cuts inland between south Wales and Somerset and narrows eastwards to a wedge, so the two landmasses are cleanly separated; the 'tidal' dot sits on that water and the 'nuclear' dot on the land of the shore to its south, and the leaders no longer end in open ocean. The ink the map was missing is there too: an even horizontal hatch of fine parallel lines now covers the whole sea and the margin around it, stops at every coastline, and leaves the land entirely clear, so land and sea are told apart by ink and not by wash. The rest of the outline stands up: Scotland with the Hebrides, the northern isles and the Moray Firth, the whole island of Ireland with the Northern Ireland border inked and only the northern part labelled, the Isle of Man, the Humber drawn as a notch with the 'natural gas' dot on it, the Norfolk bulge, the Thames estuary and the Isle of Wight. The 'offshore wind' dot sits well out in the North Sea off north-east England, the 'hydroelectric' dot in the north-west Highlands, and the 'solar' dot inland in the south-east, clearly south of the wind dot. All eight required labels are present and correctly spelled, with 'renewable' or 'non-renewable' written in ink beneath every vignette; I read the lettering on the 1536 px PNG as well as the 900 px JPEG. The redraw did cost one thing: about a 200 px stretch of the west Somerset and north Devon coast, right where the new channel was cut, has lost its ink outline and is now defined only by the edge of the sea hatch.

First attempt was a retry — gate and ink testthe Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary are absent from the map; south Wales and Somerset are drawn as continuous land (measured: unbroken land wash from x=420 to x=560 at y=435-455)

Religious Studies · Judaism: Practices

The Synagogue and Public Worship

religious-studies-aqa · lesson 1 · accent #1e40af · annotated interior of an Orthodox synagogue

The brief

The inside of an Orthodox synagogue drawn large and straight on, filling the frame: a raised reading platform with a sloping desk standing in the centre of the main hall, rows of seating surrounding it on all four sides, an ornamented cupboard set into the far wall with embroidered curtains and Torah scrolls visible inside, a single lamp burning on a chain above that cupboard, and an upper gallery running along one side wall. Warm timber, stone and embroidered fabric in their natural colours; no people in the picture.

Why a picture here
The bimah, the aron hakodesh and the ner tamid are defined in the text one after another, but their positions relative to each other and to Jerusalem are the part students are asked about and cannot picture.
Labels that must appear
bimah; aron hakodesh; ner tamid; Torah scrolls; gallery; east wall, facing Jerusalem
Facts the gate will check
  • the bimah stands in the centre of the hall with seating on all four sides of it, as in an Orthodox synagogue
  • the aron hakodesh is set into the wall labelled as facing Jerusalem
  • the ner tamid hangs above the aron hakodesh and is drawn alight
  • the Torah scrolls are inside the aron hakodesh

Vision gate & ink test

The main content note was carried out well: the bimah now stands in the open floor with a bench block against the ark wall facing the viewer, a long run down each side wall and two benches across the near edge whose panelled backs face us and whose cushions face inward, so seating surrounds the reader on all four sides as the lesson describes. The ner tamid hangs on a chain directly above the ark crest with a lit flame and glow, three dressed Torah scrolls stand inside the open ark, the gallery runs along the right side wall, and the east wall leader lands on the same far wall as the ark. The two lettering notes were not carried out: judged on the full-resolution PNG at 14x, the gold band across the curtain pelmet is still invented ornamental script with loops and curls found in no Hebrew letterform, and the red-curtain line, although drawn in well-formed Hebrew letters, reads kaf-yod / mem-tsadi-vav-final-mem / tav-vav-resh-heh, a non-word where a real phrase belongs. The label note was not carried out either: a pixel measure of the Torah scrolls label box shows 76 per cent of it over drawn matter, and the crop confirms it sits squarely on the stone wall, with aron hakodesh at 29 per cent grazing the wall edge.

First attempt was a retry — gatebimah drawn at the front against the ark platform, not in the centre of the hall

The one correction sent backMove the raised bimah platform back from the ark to the middle of the open floor and turn the rear bench block round to face it, so that benches face the bimah on all four sides and the reader stands in the centre of the hall. Also render the gold inscription on the ark curtain as REAL, correctly formed Hebrew letters, and move every label clear of the drawn wall so no label sits on top of the drawing.
  • gold inscription band on the ark curtain is still invented glyph shapes, not Hebrew (judged on the full-resolution PNG at 14x)
  • the Hebrew line on the curtain is correctly formed letters but spells a non-word, so the phrase is meaningless
  • the Torah scrolls label sits on top of the drawn stone wall, not clear of the drawing (76 per cent of its box over ink)
  • the aron hakodesh label grazes the drawn wall at its right end (29 per cent of its box over ink)
  • the far wall fades to bare paper above the ner tamid, so the lamp hangs against nothing at the top of the frame
  • House rule: real, correctly spelled lettering in the appropriate language: the curtain pelmet carries invented non-Hebrew script and the curtain line spells a non-word
  • House rule: composition rule (annotated-object): labels must sit clear of the drawing, but Torah scrolls sits on the drawn wall

Ink test. With colour gone every named part still reads: timber, stone, upholstery and the dark ark interior separate cleanly by tone, all six leaders are followable, and the Torah scrolls label, although over the wall, still carries enough contrast to read.

Chemistry · Chemistry Paper 2

Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

science-aqa · lesson 1 · accent #2563eb · hand-drawn graph of the volume of gas collected against time

The brief

A hand-drawn line graph with time on the horizontal axis in seconds, from 0 to 120, and volume of gas collected on the vertical axis in cubic centimetres, from 0 to 60. Two curves both start at the origin and both level off flat at 50 cubic centimetres. The high concentration curve rises steeply and reaches the flat at about 40 seconds; the low concentration curve rises more gently and reaches the same flat at about 100 seconds. A thin translucent wash fills the area under each curve, the low-concentration wash a paler tone of the same grey. A short straight tangent is inked on the steep part of the upper curve where the rate is fastest.

Why a picture here
The lesson states that a steeper curve means a faster rate and that changing the concentration changes the steepness but not the final volume; that is a claim about the shape of two curves, and prose cannot show a shape.
Labels that must appear
time / s; volume of gas / cm3; high concentration; low concentration; reaction complete; steepest here, fastest rate
Facts the gate will check
  • both curves finish at the same height on the volume axis, 50 cubic centimetres
  • the high concentration curve is steeper at the start and levels off earlier than the low concentration curve
  • both axes carry inked tick marks with numbers, and the scale is even along each axis
  • the two curves are told apart by their labels and by ink line style, not by colour alone

Vision gate & ink test

Both retry notes were carried out. A luminance scan across the plot finds no jump at 100 seconds, and the wash now runs from the time axis up to the curve across the whole span, fading out at the 120 mark over about ten pixels with no straight vertical edge. The vertical axis reads volume of gas / cm with a properly raised superscript three, confirmed on the full-resolution PNG. The numbers all hold: time ticks at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 evenly spaced, volume ticks 0 to 60 in tens, both curves settling on 50, the solid curve flat from about 40 seconds and the dashed one meeting the plateau with its reaction complete dot at about 102 seconds, and the tangent inked on the steep part of the upper curve at about 15 seconds. The two curves are told apart by line style, solid against dashed, with no colour doing that work.

First attempt was a retry — gatethe pale wash stops dead at a straight vertical edge at 100 s, leaving the area under the curve from 100 to 120 s unwashed and inventing a boundary that is not a data feature

The one correction sent backRedraw both washes so each one runs from the time axis up to its own curve across the whole 0 to 120 s span, deleting the straight vertical wash edge at 100 s, and raise the three in the vertical axis label to a superscript so it reads cm³.
  • the darker tone reads as a band between the two curves rather than as one flat wash under the high-concentration curve, because the paler low wash covers the area beneath the dashed curve
  • the low concentration leader lands at about 90 seconds where the dashed curve has already merged with the plateau, so the dot sits on the solid line
  • the tangent is drawn as two nearly parallel strokes, and two of the leader dots are doubled
  • House rule: composition rule (data-picture): the rule asks for one flat translucent wash per curve, but the high-concentration area carries two tones
  • House rule: composition rule (data-picture): no value is printed at a plotted point; the only figures are the axis numbers

Ink test. With colour gone the solid and dashed curves stay clearly distinct, the two wash tones remain separable from each other and from the paper, and every axis number, label and leader still reads.

The two bins, and what they argue for fresh first attempts, not third tries

Two rows could not be saved inside their two attempts, and both failed on the same kind of thing: something the ink was supposed to carry and did not. The heart cutaway told oxygenated from deoxygenated blood by wash alone, and its retry laid the corrective stipple over both sides, which distinguishes nothing. The synagogue drew the Hebrew on the ark curtain as invented glyph shapes. Each suggested an amendment to the block, so each amendment was written and tried.

The amended BRIEF, not the amended style block. biology_fix2, which names the stipple in the fact list, delivers an even round-dot ink stipple confined to the vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary artery with the oxygenated half completely clear, and it reads that way in greyscale; biology_fix, under the amended style block with the original brief, carries no stipple, hatch or dash on either side, and its greyscale copy separates the two circuits only by the labels.

A second finding fell out of it. A retry is a fresh text-to-image call, not an edit: the model re-rolls the whole picture from the corrected prompt. Twice here a correction landed and took something working away with it. A retry that must preserve part of the drawing needs the edits endpoint and the previous image as a reference, not a longer sentence.
